analysis.one_liner: Requires stronger federal safety tests to keep dressers and chests from tipping over on children.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill on June 23, 2021, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Every year, unanchored dressers and chests of drawers tip over and seriously injure or kill young children who climb on them or pull out their drawers. The STURDY Act would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to replace the existing voluntary furniture standard with a mandatory one within a year, using tests that mimic real-world conditions: a child up to 60 pounds climbing, drawers loaded with clothes, carpeted floors, and multiple open drawers. It also requires stronger warnings. The bill would have covered all freestanding clothing storage units sold in the U.S., including units under 30 inches tall that earlier standards left out.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who get dressers and chests that are tested against realistic tip-over scenarios instead of a weaker voluntary standard. The bill requires testing on all units, including shorter ones left out of prior standards.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the CPSC to write a binding safety standard for freestanding clothing storage units within one year, replacing reliance on a voluntary industry standard.
Requires tests that simulate real-world conditions: a child up to 60 pounds, drawers with items in them, multiple open drawers, carpeted floors, and dynamic force.
Extends testing to every clothing storage unit, including those under 30 inches tall, and requires warnings based on the ASTM standard, strengthened where necessary to protect children.

analysis.who_pays: Furniture manufacturers and importers bear the cost of more rigorous testing and any redesign needed to pass it; some of that cost may be passed to consumers in furniture prices. Very small and craft furniture makers face the same testing burden as large producers.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers, importers, and especially small craft furniture makers face new testing and compliance costs, which can show up in retail prices.
A statutory one-year deadline for the CPSC compresses the agency's rulemaking and leaves little room to tailor the standard if testing requirements prove unworkable for some designs.
The voluntary ASTM standard already existed; the bill's value depends on how much the mandatory, real-world testing improves on it, which the record does not quantify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety stakes are severe — tip-overs can kill small children — while the cost is a compliance and redesign burden spread across the furniture industry, some of it passed to shoppers. The main honest criticism is design rigidity: a hard one-year federal deadline is a blunt tool for an agency, and small makers bear the same burden as big ones. On the whole, the protections plausibly outweigh the costs, but the record here does not contain cost estimates or casualty data to weigh precisely.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on June 23, 2021 under a fast-track procedure used for uncontroversial bills, but the Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 24, 2021 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee.
On June 22, 2021, Chairman Pallone moved to pass the bill under suspension of the rules, a House fast-track process reserved for noncontroversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority.
The House passed the bill on June 23, 2021, bundled with more than a dozen other bills under the same suspension procedure.
The Senate received the bill on June 24, 2021 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action appears in the record.
No Senate vote ever took place, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Furniture makers and importers avoided mandatory real-world tip-over testing and any redesign costs, because the Senate never took up the bill; families with young children got no federal fix during that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Furniture makers; no federal fix enacted

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats, but the House passed the bill under suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority, indicating at least some Republican support; the record does not include a roll-call breakdown, and the Senate took no vote.

industries.note: The bill would replace a voluntary industry standard with a mandatory CPSC rule requiring realistic tip-over testing and covering shorter units previously excluded, imposing testing and potential redesign costs across the industry, costs that partly land on consumers through prices.

The bill requires consultation with craft and handmade furniture manufacturers but applies the same mandatory testing standard to them as to large producers, a heavier relative burden for small shops.
